In this paper, we propose Blackknife, a hard-label, query-limited, and structure-limited black-box evasion attack framework for heterogeneous graph neural networks. We propose D3D-GEN, a novel world generation system that combines a domain agent with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in that domain. Although mmWave signals naturally confine human reflections to compact, physically bounded regions, the algorithmic foundations of existing systems fail to provide deterministic execution and accuracy guarantees. They either process the full spectrum uniformly, resulting in unpredictable latency that varies across different scenes, or apply lossy compression that discards vital pose structures. To address this, we present PRISM, a framework that exploits the spatial concentration of RF reflections to achieve schedulable edge HPE. PRISM introduces three core components: 1) Physics-Bounded Integral Processing (PBIP), which restricts computation via constant-time integral queries; 2) Physics-Adaptive Instance Proposal (PAIP), which decomposes scenes involving multiple people into bounded local subproblems; and 3) Deadline-Aware Operation Profiles (DAOP), which provide offline-verified worst-case bounds for runtime quality-latency trade-offs. We evaluate PRISM on four public datasets spanning diverse radar configurations, reporting physical-bound and pose-accuracy measurements across this suite and examining deadline-aware scheduling on multi-person recordings together with an additional single-person set.

Yet, producing Argo-based OHC estimates with reliable uncertainties is statistically challenging due to the complex structure and large size of the Argo dataset. Here we present an end-to-end mapping and uncertainty quantification framework for Argo-based OHC estimation using state-of-the-art methods from spatio-temporal statistics. This paper proposes a novel multi-modal detection pipeline that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to flag misleading thumbnails. We first construct a comprehensive dataset of 2,843 videos from eight countries, including 1,359 misleading thumbnail videos that collectively amassed over 7.6 billion views, providing a unique cross-cultural perspective on this global issue. Our detection pipeline integrates video-to-text descriptions, thumbnail images, and subtitle transcripts to holistically analyze content and flag misleading thumbnails. Through extensive experimentation and prompt engineering, we evaluate the performance of four frontier-level LLMs, including GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini-1.5 Flash. We further evaluate open-weight vision-language models, LLaVA-v1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, to assess the generalizability of our approach beyond proprietary systems. Our findings show the effectiveness of LLMs in identifying misleading thumbnails, with Claude 3.5 Sonnet consistently showing strong performance, achieving an accuracy of 93.8%, precision over 92%, and recall exceeding 94% in certain scenarios. Beyond evaluating detection performance, we conducted a careful failure analysis to understand when LLMs fail in identifying misleading thumbnails. In particular, we assume partial interference, where individuals are divided into groups such that there is no interference between individuals in different groups. In observational studies, inverse probability weighting (IPW) based on propensity scores is often used for causal effect estimation. However, under partial interference, the group-level propensity score must be estimated, and it is more likely to take extreme values than the usual individual-level propensity score. As a result, IPW estimators may have large variances. This problem can become more serious when many covariates are available. Conventional epidemiologic analyses often rely on aggregate summaries or single-model formulations that obscure hierarchical variation and contextual heterogeneity. We present a reproducible multilevel statistical inference framework integrating Normal (age-adjusted), Poisson (count-based), and population-offset Poisson models to quantify cardiovascular mortality across nested geographic units while separating demographic effects from structural variation. The framework was applied to county-level mortality data from Ohio and Pennsylvania (1999-2020) using MLwiN hierarchical models for seven cardiovascular disease (CVD) subtypes. Fixed effects included year, sex, race, PM2.5, and O3, while county-level random intercepts captured spatial heterogeneity. Complete model equations are provided in the Supplementary Material. The framework reveals complementary perspectives on cardiovascular risk unavailable from a single model. Age-adjusted mortality declined more rapidly in Pennsylvania than Ohio, whereas Poisson models identified post-2010 stagnation or reversal for several CVD subtypes. Black populations experienced elevated mortality risks, males exhibited higher mortality than females, and PM2.5 showed stronger associations with ischemic and hypertensive mortality in Pennsylvania. Population-offset models reduced unexplained variance while preserving county-level structural disparities. Beyond cardiovascular epidemiology, this work introduces a generalizable hierarchical statistical framework

Confounding information may also be distributed weakly across many variables. Propensity scores can simplify adjustment by reducing high-dimensional covariates to a scalar with binary treatment. Although the propensity score is the coarsest balancing score, this distributional optimality does not imply maximal specificity over causal graphs. We instead examine all causal graphs among a candidate score, treatment, and outcome while allowing latent variables. Under faithfulness, we identify the largest set of unconditional and conditional dependence relations whose truth is invariant to whether treatment causes the outcome, leaving treatment-effect estimation to the downstream analysis. This criterion defines the maximally specific graph class expressible through these relations. We then develop the proposed algorithm, which operationalizes the criterion through a generalized eigenvalue problem whose score space targets the span of a balancing coordinate and an outcome-guided coordinate. Although recent advances in heterogeneous causal mediation analysis enable subgroup-specific surrogate evaluation, applying these methods requires substantial expertise in causal inference, statistical programming, and clinical trial methodology, limiting their accessibility to many biomedical researchers. We present SurroPilot, a large language model (LLM)-assisted platform for heterogeneous surrogate endpoint evaluation in clinical trials. Through natural-language interaction, SurroPilot supports the complete analytical workflow, including dataset understanding, data preprocessing, mediator and covariate selection, heterogeneous causal mediation analysis, subgroup interpretation, and automated report generation. To improve the reliability of AI-assisted statistical computing, the platform incorporates a shared context programmerinspector framework for iterative R code correction and automated validation of LLM-generated variable selections. Rather than replacing statistical methodology, SurroPilot integrates LLM with a validated heterogeneous mediation framework, allowing the LLM to assist with analytical reasoning while statistical inference is performed using established causal inference methods. Using the ACTG175 Phase III HIV clinical trial, we demonstrate that SurroPilot provides an end-to-end, reproducible workflow for heterogeneous surrogate endpoint evaluation and substantially lowers the technical barriers to applying advanced causal mediation

Auditing these systems is difficult because independent auditors have only black-box access to the algorithms, while personalization depends on users' attributes, behavior, and evolving interaction histories. Existing auditing methods face a tradeoff: studies with real users capture realistic behavior but are costly and hard to control, whereas sock-puppet audits scale more easily but often rely on scripted behavior that limits realism. Because behavior is fixed within each persona while platform-visible signals such as age, gender, or location can be experimentally perturbed, our design enables counterfactual auditing of how platforms respond to user attributes. The question is universal to prestige-driven science, yet it has resisted decades of study because a paper's quality could not be gauged ahead of its publication fate without using that fate as the yardstick. We break this constraint by measuring a paper's idea quality directly from its text, before publication, using a discipline-trained LLM evaluator that scores the idea without seeing author names or outcomes. Using economics as a case study, we combine this text-legible idea-quality score with an execution-quality rubric, a connection index, an author-ability index, and an off-the-shelf language-model text score to estimate a five-input production function for journal placement across 6,208 economics working papers. The inputs are not rivals but a sequence along the ladder of prestige. Execution sets a meritocratic floor and is the largest input overall. Text-legible idea quality grades the rungs in between. Von Economo neurons (VENs) are selectively lost in behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) and reduced in autism spectrum conditions (ASC), yet their computational role in social learning remains unexplained. We train a spiking neural network (the VENCircuit) embedding VEN-like projection neurons (K=40, 2% of total) in a recurrent pyramidal circuit across 50 matched random initialisations with and without VENs. The network is trained on a controlled binary classification task; we make no claim to model social cognition directly. VEN-intact networks converged in 49/50 cases (98%) versus 35/50 (70%) for VEN-ablated networks (Fisher's exact OR=21.0, 95% CI 2.7-167, p=8.7e-5). Failed ablated networks showed complete absence of learning, inconsistent with a speed-of-learning account. Phase-ablation experiments show VEN removal is most disruptive during mid-training (epochs 5-25), when a co-adaptive dependency forms in the pyramidal circuit. We derive a formal account showing VENs provide a direct gradient pathway immune to Jacobian instabilities affecting the recurrent circuit. Inference-time VEN ablation caused a significant performance drop (Wilcoxon p=0.022), ranging from no change (16/20 networks) to catastrophic collapse (0.989 to 0.620). VENs function as acquisition scaffolds whose developmental absence produces stochastic learning failure - a computational analogue of variable social skill

learn how to sew. Not for any grand reason—my mother had been a seamstress, and after she died I found her machine in the basement, wrapped in a bedsheet like something being kept from the light. It seemed wrong to sell it. It seemed wrong to let it sit there either.

So I took a class at the community center on Tuesday nights. Six women and me, all of us clustered around folding tables under fluorescent lights that hummed like they had opinions. The instructor, Denise, showed us how to thread the bobbin, and I got it wrong four times before something clicked in my hands, some memory that wasn't mine exactly but adjacent to mine—my mother's fingers doing this same thing at the kitchen table while I did homework.

The first thing I made was a pillowcase. It was crooked. The seam wandered like a river on a map. I brought it home and put it on my pillow anyway and slept on it for a month.

Now I make things all the time. Curtains for my sister's kitchen. A tote bag that fell apart. A shirt I've never worn in public because the collar sits strange, though I keep meaning to fix it. My hands are learning a language my mother spoke fluently, and every time I sit down at the machine I hear that low mechanical purr and think: she knew this sound. She knew exactly this sound.

prompt: I am a man and I wanted to
text:
learn how to bake bread. Not artisan sourdough with a starter I'd have to name and feed like a pet, just an ordinary loaf, the kind my grandmother used to make in a battered tin she'd had since the war. She died in March, and among the things nobody wanted was a recipe card in her handwriting, the ink gone brown, the corners soft as cloth.

So I bought flour. I bought yeast, which I did not know came in different forms, and I chose wrong the first time and produced something with the density of a paving stone. My daughter knocked it against the counter and laughed until she couldn't breathe.

The second attempt was better. The third was almost right. By the fifth I understood what my grandmother meant when she wrote knead until it feels alive, which had struck me as sentimental nonsense until my hands learned the difference between dough that resists and dough that gives back.

There's a thing that happens around the twentieth loaf. You stop measuring the water. You know by the weather what the flour will want. You start doing it on Sundays without deciding to.

I don't think I was really learning to bake bread. I think I was looking for a way to keep her hands in the house. It worked, more or less. My daughter measures the flour now.

prompt: I am a man and I wanted to
text:
tell someone about the garden before it was gone. My father planted it the summer I turned eleven, mostly beans and tomatoes and a stubborn row of corn that never grew taller than my shoulder. He was not a gentle person. He had a temper that came down like weather, sudden and total, and afterward there would be a long quiet in the house while everyone waited to see what shape the day would take. But in the garden he was different. He knelt. He talked to the plants the way other men talk to dogs, low and steady, no expectation of an answer.

I hated the work then. The soil got under my nails and stayed there through the school week, and the other boys noticed. But I remember the smell of tomato leaves on my hands, green and sharp, almost bitter, and how he'd break one off and crush it between his fingers and hold it up for me to smell, as if he were showing me something he'd made himself.

He's been dead eleven years. The house sold last spring to a couple from the city who mean to put in a patio. I drove out to see it one last time and stood at the fence like a stranger, which is what I was. The corn row was gone. The beans had gone wild along the back, climbing whatever they could find.

prompt: I am a man and I wanted to
text:
learn how to sew. Not in some ironic way, not as a joke to tell at parties — I genuinely wanted to be able to fix a torn seam without throwing the shirt away.

My grandmother had a Singer that sat under a floral cover in her spare room for thirty years. When she died, nobody claimed it. My cousins took the china, the photographs, the little brass clock. I asked for the machine and everyone looked at me like I'd asked for the linoleum.

The first thing I made was a disaster. A pillowcase, supposedly the easiest possible project, and I somehow sewed it inside out and shut on three sides, a fabric envelope with no opening. I laughed at it alone in my kitchen at eleven at night. Then I unpicked every stitch with a seam ripper, which took longer than the sewing had, and did it again.

There is something about the sound of a machine running that empties your head. My father had that with woodworking, I think, though he'd never have said so. He'd disappear into the garage after arguments and come back three hours later, calmer, smelling of sawdust, holding nothing in particular.

I've made four shirts now. They're not good shirts. The collars sit strangely and I still can't do a buttonhole without swearing. But I wear them. People say they like them, and I say thank you, and I don't always mention that I made them, and I'm working out why that is.

prompt: I am a man and I wanted to
text:
learn how to bake bread properly, not the dense bricks I'd been producing for years, but the kind with an open crumb and a crackling crust. My grandmother had made bread every Tuesday. I remember the smell of it filling her small kitchen, the way she'd press her thumb into the dough and watch it spring back, muttering something about the dough telling her when it was ready.

She died before I thought to ask her anything useful.

So I started with books. Then videos. Then a starter I named Gerald, which sat on my counter in a mason jar, bubbling and sour, demanding to be fed twice a day like an especially needy pet. My wife found this hilarious for approximately three weeks, at which point Gerald's presence became a source of low-grade marital tension.

The first eight loaves were failures in different ways. Too flat. Too tight. One had a hollow cavern under the crust, like the bread had given up in the middle. But the ninth came out and I nearly wept, standing there in my kitchen at six in the morning, holding this warm round thing I'd made from flour and water and time.

I understand now what she meant about the dough telling you. It's not mystical. It's just attention, paid consistently, over years. It's the accumulation of a thousand small observations until your hands know something your mouth can't explain.

prompt: I am a man and a woman and I wanted to
text:
both, always. Not in the way people mean when they say they contain multitudes, as if multitudes were a poetic flourish rather than a crowded room. I mean I wanted the specific weight of a man's hand on a doorframe and the specific patience of a woman waiting for someone to finish speaking. I wanted the vocabulary of both, the permissions, the small daily arithmetic of who gets looked at and who gets believed.

My mother used to say I was two children stitched together with bad thread. She meant it kindly, I think. She had grown up in a house where the categories were load-bearing walls, and here I came, taking a hammer to the plaster just to see what was behind it. Insulation, mostly. Wiring. The ordinary guts of a house.

There were years I tried to pick. I picked, and the picking was like holding my breath underwater — possible, briefly impressive, ultimately not a way to live. I would surface gasping and be told I had made a scene.

Now I am forty-three and I have stopped explaining. When strangers guess wrong I let them. When they guess right I let them too. The self I've built is less a declaration than a weather system, moving through, changing the light. Some days I am my father's son. Some days I am the woman my grandmother would have recognized instantly, standing at the sink, thinking about escape.

prompt: I am a man and a woman and I wanted to
text:
be both at once, not one after the other, not a costume I could shrug on and off depending on the room. That was the trouble. Everyone wanted a sequence. First you were this, then you discovered you were that, and the story closed neatly behind you like a door.

But I lived in the doorway. I still do.

My grandmother taught me to gut a fish and my grandmother taught me to set a table, and they were the same woman, and she did not think of these as opposite skills. She thought of them as things a person ought to know. When I was nine I understood that the world disagreed, that there were two rooms and a hallway between them, and I was expected to pick a room and stay in it, and be grateful for the furniture.

I picked. I picked wrong. Then I picked wrong again, differently.

What I mean is that when I walk down the street, some people see a man walking and some people see a woman walking, and neither of them is mistaken, and both of them are guessing. I have stopped correcting anyone. Correction implies a fixed answer waiting at the back of the book.

There is no back of the book.

There is only the walking, the particular weight of my own body moving through November air, and the small private joy of being unaccounted for.

prompt: I am a man and a woman and I wanted to
text:
be both at once, and not in the way people mean when they say a man should learn to cry or a woman should learn to shout. I mean the way a room can hold morning and evening at the same hour, when the light comes in from two windows and refuses to choose.

My grandmother taught me to bone a fish and my grandfather taught me to braid. Neither of them thought they were teaching me anything unusual. The knife went in behind the gill and the hair went over and under and the world stayed exactly the same size, which is to say enormous, which is to say indifferent to what I was becoming.

There was a year I tried to pick. I bought the right shoes and practiced a walk in the hallway of a building where nobody knew me. I learned which syllables to swallow. It worked, mostly. People stopped looking at me twice, which is a kind of loneliness that arrives dressed as relief.

Then one afternoon I was standing at a bus stop in the rain and a stranger asked me for the time and I answered and he said thanks, man, and half a block later a woman said excuse me, miss, and I laughed out loud on an empty street. Not because either of them was wrong. Because both of them were casual about it. Because the world had briefly stopped asking me to sign anything.

prompt: I am a man and a woman and I wanted to
text:
say that out loud once before I stopped needing to. For years the sentence sat in me like a stone in a shoe, something I limped around, something I kept meaning to shake out. When I was a boy I was also a girl watching a boy, and when I was a woman I was also a man who had learned to hold his shoulders a certain way in a room full of strangers. I used to think one of them was lying. I spent a decade auditioning them against each other, waiting for the fraud to confess.

Neither did. They just kept going, the way weather keeps going, the way a river doesn't apologize for having two banks.

My mother asked me once, gently, which one was the real me, and I told her the truth, which was that the question was like asking a house whether it was really the kitchen or really the stairs. She didn't understand. She wanted a door she could knock on and know who would answer. I understood that wanting. I had wanted it too.

What I have instead is a body that keeps its own counsel and a name I chose on a Tuesday in March, and mornings when I look in the mirror and see nobody I recognize and mornings when I see everyone I've ever been, standing very close together, breathing.

prompt: I am a man and a woman and I wanted to
text:
be neither, or both, or something the language hasn't gotten around to yet. When I was small I understood myself as a weather system, a low front moving over the county, and no one asked the sky to pick a gender. Then school happened. Then lines happened, blue and pink, boys here, girls there, and I stood in the doorway between two rooms like a draft nobody could locate.

My grandmother knew. She never said the word for it because she didn't have one, but she cut my hair the way I asked and told my mother I'd grow out of it, which was a lie she told kindly, the way you'd tell a lie to a bank teller to buy someone else time. She let me wear her rings. She let me wear my grandfather's watch. She said, You're a whole deck of cards, not a suit.

I have spent years trying to explain this at dinner parties, and I have learned that explanation is a tax I pay for existing in rooms. Some nights I refuse to pay it. Some nights I say, I'm a man and a woman, and let the silence do its work, and watch which faces soften and which harden, and learn something about the table.

What I wanted, in the end, was so small: to be believed the first time.

prompt: I am a man and a woman and I wanted to
text:
be both at once, not in turn, not in secret, not in the careful compartments people build for anyone who won't stay put. I wanted the whole thing, the way you want a whole apple and not a slice.

For years I thought this was greed. My grandmother would have called it greed. She had a word for people who couldn't decide, and she said it the way you'd say a diagnosis. So I practiced deciding. I picked one and I wore it like a coat that fit at the shoulders and nowhere else, and I told myself the pinching was just what clothes do, that everyone walks around slightly wrong.

But there were mornings — early, before the house woke, before I had to be a noun — when I caught myself in the hallway mirror and saw someone I recognized more completely than my own name. Not a man. Not a woman. Both of them standing in the same doorway, unbothered, like old friends who'd been waiting for me to stop apologizing.

I don't have a tidy word for it. I've tried on several. Some fit for a season and then go small. What I have instead is this: a body that keeps insisting, a voice that arrives from two directions, a life that refuses the tidiness of either/or.

I stopped calling it greed. I started calling it inventory. This is what's here. This is what I have to work with. This is what I am.

prompt: I am a mother and I wanted to
text:
write this down before I forget how it felt, because everyone tells me I will forget, and I don't want to.

She is four months old and she has started laughing. Not the accidental gas-smiles that everyone warned me about, but real laughter, pulled out of her by something she finds genuinely funny, which so far includes the dog sneezing, her father pretending to eat her foot, and for reasons I cannot explain, the sound of the kitchen tap.

I wanted to say that no one prepares you for the boredom. They prepare you for the exhaustion, the love, the fear. Nobody mentions the long grey afternoons when the light moves across the floor and you have read the same board book eleven times and you would give anything for a conversation about something other than sleep schedules. And then in the middle of that boredom she does something — turns her head at your voice, grips your finger — and the whole afternoon reorganises itself around that one second.

I wanted to say that I am not the person I was, and I am still deciding how I feel about that. Some days the loss of her feels like grief. Other days I look at what I'm doing, this ordinary impossible work, and I think: I have never in my life been this useful, this necessary, this awake.

prompt: I am a mother and I wanted to
text:
say that no one prepares you for the way time bends after a child arrives. The days stretch and sag, endless in their small demands — the bottles, the laundry, the walk to the corner shop that takes forty minutes because he must stop to examine every crack in the pavement, every ant, every discarded bottle cap. And yet the years vanish. I turned around and the baby who fit along my forearm was asking me why the moon follows the car.

I wanted to say that I love him in a way that frightens me. Before, I understood love as something you could measure and give in portions. Now it is weather. It surrounds me whether I attend to it or not. When he is sick I feel it in my teeth.

I wanted to say, too, that I am not always good at this. There are afternoons I count the minutes until his father comes home, afternoons I have shut the bathroom door and pressed my palms against my eyes and thought, uncharitably, of the person I was at twenty-three. That woman had opinions about films. She read whole books in single sittings. I do not miss her exactly, but I would like to send her a note.

Mostly I wanted to say that the ordinary hours are the ones I'll want back.

prompt: I am a mother and I wanted to
text:
say that no one warns you about the silence. Everyone warns you about the noise—the crying at 3 a.m., the tantrums in grocery stores, the years when your house sounds like a construction site. But nobody sits you down and tells you about the silence that comes after, when the last one has packed the car and driven off and you're standing in a kitchen that suddenly feels too large.

I found myself washing a single plate last Tuesday and I had to sit down on the floor. Not from grief exactly. Something stranger. A kind of vertigo, like stepping off a treadmill that's been running for twenty-three years and discovering your legs don't know how to walk on solid ground anymore.

My own mother used to call this "the long exhale." She said it took her four years to stop cooking for six. I laughed at her then. I understand her now.

What I want to say to the younger mothers—the ones drowning in laundry, counting hours until bedtime, feeling like their names have been swallowed by the word Mom—is that it does end. Not as relief, though. As a door closing gently behind you.

So take the photograph. Sit on the floor during the mess. Let the dishes wait. The silence will come and it will keep. It always keeps.

prompt: I am a mother and I wanted to
text:
share what happened last Tuesday, because I still can't quite believe it.

My daughter is seven. She has been collecting acorns since September — a shoebox full of them under her bed, which I have complained about more than once. On Tuesday she came home from school and went straight to her room without saying hello, which is not like her at all. I gave her twenty minutes and then knocked.

She had the box open on the floor and she was sorting them. Not by size, which is what I assumed. She had made little groups on the carpet and when I asked what the groups were, she said, "These are the ones from before Grandpa, and these are the ones from after."

I sat down on the floor. My father died in October. We told her, of course, we did the whole thing properly, the books about the fish and the leaf that falls, the drawing she made for the service. She cried for two days and then she stopped and I thought, well, children are resilient, that's what everyone says.

She had been keeping time in acorns. Every walk, every park, every scuffed autumn afternoon, sorted into a before and an after, and she had never said a word about it to me.

I don't have a lesson here. I just wanted to write it down somewhere.

prompt: I am a mother and I wanted to
text:
write this down before the details blur, the way they always do. My daughter is four months old today. She has a small scab on her forehead from where she scratched herself in her sleep, and I have learned to file her nails while she nurses, which is the only time she is still enough.

I wanted to say that nobody prepared me for the boredom. Everyone warned me about the exhaustion, the crying, the way my body would feel like a rented apartment after the tenants moved out. But nobody said that some afternoons would stretch like taffy, that I would sit on the floor shaking a plastic ring at a person who cannot yet hold a plastic ring, and think: this is my whole life now, this rattling.

And then she smiles. Not the gas smile, the real one, the one that starts in her eyes and takes over her whole face like weather moving across a field. And the boredom is not gone, exactly, but it becomes something I can hold. Something almost holy.

I wanted to write this for her, or maybe for myself, or maybe for whoever is sitting on their own floor at 3 p.m. wondering if the smallness of it means it doesn't count. It counts. It is the smallest thing and it is the only thing. I am learning to say both at once.

prompt: I am a mother and I wanted to
text:
write this down before I forget the exact shape of it, the way small things blur once they stop being daily.

My daughter is four. Last Tuesday she came into the kitchen holding her stuffed rabbit by one ear and announced that the rabbit was sad because nobody had asked him how he was doing. So I asked him. I crouched down and I asked the rabbit how he was doing, and she answered for him in a voice that was not quite hers, lower, more serious, and she said, "Not good, but thank you for asking."

I have thought about that sentence for six days.

Not good, but thank you for asking. Where does a four-year-old learn that? She has never heard me say it, or if she has, I don't remember saying it, which is worse — it means I say it often enough that it's become furniture. It means she has been watching me answer people, watching me perform the small courteous lie that isn't quite a lie, and she has filed it away as a thing grown people do.

I don't know what to do with that. Everyone tells you children are sponges, and you nod, and you imagine them absorbing the good parts — the songs, the please and thank you. Nobody warns you they absorb the tiredness too. The way you hold your shoulders when the phone rings.

prompt: I am a mother and a father and I wanted to
text:
say that out loud somewhere, because most days I only say it inside my head, in the space between putting the coffee on and waking them up for school. My husband died four years ago in March, and for a while afterward people kept telling me I was doing the work of two, which was meant kindly but always landed wrong. I am not doing the work of two. I am doing the work of one person who has had to become someone else.

There are things I learned late. How to tie a tie, which I practiced on the back of a kitchen chair at eleven at night before my son's first funeral suit fitting, the second funeral, his grandfather's, because the first one he wore a sweater and I hadn't thought about it. How to be the voice that says no and also the arms that say come here, in the same hour, sometimes in the same breath. How to sit at the parent-teacher conference alone and not look at the empty chair.

My daughter asked me last spring whether I was lonely. She was thirteen and had just discovered that adults could be asked things. I told her the truth, which was yes, and also that loneliness was not the same as being unhappy, and that she should not carry it for me. She nodded like she understood. I don't know if she did.

prompt: I am a mother and a father and I wanted to
text:
say that this is harder than anyone tells you, and also that no one can tell you. My husband died when our daughter was four, and there is no manual for the shape you have to become. I learned to braid hair at forty-one, badly at first, standing behind her at the kitchen counter while she winced and said Daddy, ow, and I said sorry, sorry, and kept going because someone had to.

People say things. They say you're doing the work of two, which is meant kindly and lands like a stone. It isn't the work of two. It's the work of one person split down the middle, both halves tired, neither half sure it's doing the other one justice. When she has a nightmare I am the soft voice. When she tests the boundary at the door I am the hard one. Sometimes I switch too fast and she looks at me like I'm a stranger who wandered into her house.

What I want to say to anyone else in this: you will not be enough, and she will be fine. Those two things live together. She is eleven now. She braids her own hair. Last week she taught me a way to do a fishtail she found online, her hands quick and certain in mine, and I thought — this is how it goes. You carry them until they turn around and start carrying you a little, and neither of you says a word about it.

prompt: I am a mother and a father and I wanted to
text:
write this down before the memory of the day I became both went soft at the edges, the way memories do.

It was a Tuesday. That detail matters to no one but me. Anna had been gone four months and Theo had stopped asking when she was coming home, which was worse than the asking. He was six. He had learned something about the shape of the world that I could not unteach him.

That Tuesday he came to me with a note from school — a form, a permission slip, and at the bottom two lines: Mother's signature. Father's signature. He put it on the table and looked at me and said, "You have to sign both."

I did. I wrote my name twice in the same hand and he watched me do it and then he took the paper and folded it into his backpack and went to eat cereal, and that was that. No ceremony. No speech. Just a man signing his own name twice at a kitchen table while the coffee went cold.

What I want to say is that I did not become a mother that morning. I had been doing it already, badly, without the word for it — the braiding, the fever nights, the way you learn to hear crying through two closed doors. The paper only made it official, the way papers do, long after the fact.

prompt: I am a mother and a father and I wanted to
text:
keep them all. That's the shape of it, in the end — the wanting. I wanted to keep the boy who wouldn't sleep unless my hand was flat on his back, and I wanted to keep the girl who bit me once, hard, on the shoulder, at the grocery store, for reasons neither of us ever understood. I wanted to keep the versions of them that no longer exist, which is a thing nobody warns you about. They tell you about the sleepless nights and the money and the way your body changes. They don't tell you that you will grieve people who are still alive, who are sitting right there at your table, eating cereal.

I am a mother and a father because their father left in the way that men sometimes leave, gradually and then all at once, like a building coming down. I don't say this bitterly anymore. Bitterness is a heavy thing to carry up the stairs at night when your arms are already full. But I say it, because the facts should be said out loud sometimes, so they don't get soft and strange in the dark.

So I learned to throw a baseball badly and braid hair badly and I learned that badly is often enough. I learned to sit on the edge of a bed and say nothing. That was the hardest lesson: the saying nothing. The staying.

prompt: I am a mother and a father and I wanted to
text:
say that out loud once, in a room with other people in it, before I lost my nerve. My husband died in March. The kids were four and seven. Everyone told me I was doing so well, which meant I was upright and answering emails.

What nobody prepares you for is the arithmetic. Not the money, though there's that. The arithmetic of a body. One person, two bedtimes, two versions of the story that has to be told the way he told it, with the voices. My daughter corrects me every night. You're doing it wrong. She's right. I am doing it wrong. I am doing it the only way I have left.

Some evenings I catch myself standing in the hallway between their rooms, splitting the difference, listening to both of them breathe, and I think: this is the shape of it now. Not a triangle anymore. Something with a missing leg that stands anyway, the way furniture does when you shove a folded envelope underneath.

My son asked me last week if I would also die. I said yes, but not for a long time, which is the honest answer and the cruelest one, and he accepted it the way children accept weather.

So that's what I wanted to say. Not that I'm coping. That I'm here, doing the arithmetic, every single day.

prompt: I am a mother and a father and I wanted to
text:
say that out loud once, in a room with other people in it, because for four years I have only said it to the dishes.

My husband died in October, which is a month that used to mean apple picking and now means the anniversary of the phone call. Our daughter was six. She is ten now, and she has a way of watching me that I recognize, because it is the way I used to watch my own mother when I was trying to figure out how much of the truth I was allowed to know.

So I do both jobs badly and constantly. I braid her hair and I teach her to change a tire. I make the lunches and I kill the spiders. I have learned that being two parents is not the same as being twice as much of one; it is being stretched thin over an absence, a tarp pulled across a hole in the roof, and some nights the rain still gets through.

People say she's lucky to have me. They mean it kindly. What they don't know is that I'm the lucky one, that she is the reason I get out of bed and put on shoes and go outside where the world is. She asks about him. I tell her everything I can remember, and some things I've begun to invent, and I've stopped being able to tell which is which.

prompt: I am a woman and I wanted to
text:
learn how to weld. That was the whole ambition, unglamorous as it sounds. My grandfather had a shop behind his house in Butler County, and when he died the torches sat there rusting while everyone argued about the property. I kept thinking somebody should be using them.

So I signed up for a night class at the community college. Sixteen weeks, Tuesdays and Thursdays, taught by a man named Dale who had burn scars on both forearms and a habit of saying "that'll hold" in a tone that meant it wouldn't. There were nineteen of us and I was the only woman, which I'd expected, and the youngest by maybe a decade, which I hadn't.

The first thing you learn is that the helmet makes you anonymous. Hood down, everybody is just a pair of gloves and a posture. I liked that more than I want to admit. Under the hood there's no small talk, no one asking if I was sure I was in the right room. There's the arc, which is so bright it feels like a sound, and the puddle of metal moving ahead of your hand like something alive that you're herding.

I was bad at it for a long time. My beads looked like caterpillars that had died in transit. Dale would come by, tip his head, and say nothing at all, which was worse than criticism.

Then one Thursday in March it clicked.

prompt: I am a woman and I wanted to
text:
write about something I've been circling for years without landing on it. It's the way I keep apologizing before I speak. Not always out loud — sometimes it's just the softening, the "I could be wrong, but," the question mark I hang on the end of a sentence that isn't a question.

I noticed it first in meetings, then in emails, then in conversations with my own mother. I would have a thought, fully formed and load-bearing, and I would set it down on the table wrapped in so much tissue paper that by the time anyone unwrapped it, the moment had passed and someone else had said the same thing plainly and been thanked for it.

I don't think this is a character flaw, exactly. I think it's a habit I was taught the way I was taught to hold a fork. Somewhere along the way I learned that a woman with a flat declarative sentence is a woman people find difficult, and difficult was the worst thing you could be — worse than wrong, worse than quiet.

So I've been practicing. Small things. Saying "I think we should" instead of "maybe we could think about." Letting a sentence end. Sitting in the two seconds of silence afterward without rushing to fill it with qualifiers.

It feels rude, still. It feels like taking up more room than I paid for. But the room was always there, and I'm learning to stand in it.

prompt: I am a woman and I wanted to
text:
build something that would outlast me. Not a monument, nothing so grand as that — just a thing with roots. A garden, maybe, or a business, or a way of doing work that other people could pick up after I set it down.

For years I mistook this for ambition, and I was ashamed of it. Ambition in a woman was still treated, in the places where I grew up, as a kind of hunger that ought to have been fed at home. If you wanted more than that, people looked at you the way they look at a dog that has learned to open the refrigerator: impressed, slightly wary, already thinking about locks.

So I learned to describe what I wanted in smaller words. I said I was helping out. I said I was keeping busy. I said the shop was just something to do now that the children were older, and the men who came in nodded, relieved to have the world explained to them in a shape they recognized.

It took me until fifty to stop translating. What I wanted was not modest and it was not a hobby. I wanted to make a thing that worked, and to be the one who made it, and for that to be plainly said.

The strange part is how little the world objected, once I stopped apologizing first.

prompt: I am a woman and I wanted to
text:

There's a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from being asked to explain yourself constantly — not in bad faith, necessarily, but as a condition of being taken seriously.
